target.thesis: Gubelmann's Kantian criterion has no principled stopping point at the skin without biological chauvinism. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines, it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting whole, so 'LLMs cannot speak' reduces to 'parts as such do not speak'. The whole may be a speaker, with authorship layered across levels and fixed by a separate attribution rule. A distinct third kind of author is not established.
target.headline: Gubelmann's Kantian criterion of organismhood, on which parts are reciprocally means and ends and the whole organises and maintains itself, does not fix a level of attribution. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting system. This turns 'LLMs cannot speak' into the trivial claim that organs do not speak, and it yields a speech-act author that is neither the LLM nor a human proxy.
target.target: Gubelmann's organismic ground. It also targets proxy accounts (Green and Michel; Arora), which assume the author must be an individual human.
target.sketch: For Kant a natural purpose is a whole whose parts exist for and through one another. Nothing in that definition privileges the skin-bounded individual. Firms, newsrooms and customer-service operations are self-organising and self-maintaining through hiring, repair and revenue. Within them, deployed LLMs are retrained, patched and rewarded according to the whole's goals, and their outputs figure in the whole's reproduction of its own conditions. If goals set by such a whole count as autonomously set, which Gubelmann's cognitive-autonomy concession for LLMs invites, then speech acts through LLMs are performed by the whole and by no part. This differs from the proxy view, because no single human principal is the author and no individual's intention is being relayed. It also differs from Gubelmann's denial, because the speech act is genuine and the whole has the intentions. The premise the argument turns on is that his three-way separation of material, cognitive and moral autonomy can be satisfied at the level of an assemblage. He cannot rule that out without an independent principle of individuation, and Kant supplies none. His reply that only biological individuals qualify would restore the biological chauvinism he elsewhere disclaims.

findings.part: Gubelmann's organismic ground, and the premise that he disclaims biological chauvinism and concedes some cognitive autonomy to LLMs
findings.source: Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now): A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case", Philosophy & Technology 37:32, 2024
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="3-5">Agents with intentions need to be autonomous organisms, while LLMs are heteronomous mechanisms.</cite> He also suggests <cite index="64-9">transformer-based LLMs might be first steps toward non-biological organisms, which could overturn the Kantian organism/mechanism distinction.</cite> He grants that during training <cite index="66-1,66-2">there was never an explicit decision by the human engineer about which part of the mechanism does the task.</cite> On material autonomy he says <cite index="4-1">LLMs have none; they do not care about their continued existence.</cite>
findings.note: The target holds the ascribed view and explicitly leaves room for non-biological organisms, which the thesis can use as its premise. I saw only search snippets of the full text and found no passage on assemblages or firms.

findings.part: The claim that proxy accounts (Green & Michel; Arora) assume the author must be an individual human
findings.source: Arora, "Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions", Philosophy & Technology 37:15, 2024; Gubelmann 2024 on Green & Michel 2022; Synthese 2026 "Who asserts when no one asserts?"
findings.what_they_say: Arora holds that <cite index="14-4">only machine utterances count as proxy assertions where the epistemic responsibility of designers, or a collective of actors whose work influences the utterance, can be tied back to them.</cite> Gubelmann reports that Green & Michel analyse a <cite index="12-8,12-9">council representative who performs a speech act by assuming the role of representative of that council.</cite> A 2026 survey describes the proxy view as tracing accountability <cite index="10-4">to the human agents or organizations behind the system.</cite>
findings.note: Proxy views already allow organizational or collective principals, so 'individual human' overstates them. A 2026 Synthese piece reports Arora requiring a conscious principal (22-9), so the charge may still hold for Arora. I saw only snippets and a secondhand report of Green & Michel, so the thesis should restate the contrast.

findings.part: Whether any independent principle of individuation is available (the thesis says Kant supplies none and Gubelmann has none)
findings.source: Weber & Varela, "Life after Kant: Natural purposes and the autopoietic foundations of biological individuality", Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences, 2002; Maturana/Varela caution as reported on social autopoiesis
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="40-7,40-8">Kant's natural purposes converge with autopoiesis on an immanent teleology tied to the self-establishment of an identity that is the living process.</cite> A secondhand summary says <cite index="68-10">Maturana and Varela argue that extending autopoiesis to social systems reduces it to a metaphor.</cite>
findings.note: This tradition supplies a candidate individuation principle (self-produced identity, organizational closure) that Gubelmann could invoke against firms. It is a rival to answer, not a closure, because I did not see an argument that firms fail it. The Maturana/Varela caution is secondhand.

findings.part: No principled stopping point at the skin
findings.source: "The necessity of extended autopoiesis", Adaptive Behavior (author and year not shown in result)
findings.what_they_say: The abstract argues that <cite index="65-8">the significance of the spatial boundary in autopoiesis has been overstated.</cite> It also says <cite index="65-5">the network should be thought of as extending beyond the boundaries of the body.</cite>
findings.note: It shows an organisational account of life can reject skin-bounded individuation, which is evidence for the thesis. The same snippet also ties cogniser individuality to autonomy, so it is not a straightforward ally.

findings.part: The whole (organization) can be the speaker, with authorship layered across human and nonhuman parts and fixed by an attribution rule
findings.source: Brummans & Cooren, "Approaches to the Communicative Constitution of Organizations", Sage Handbook of Organizational Communication, 2014; Schoeneborn et al., "The Communicative Constitution of Organization, Organizing, and Organizationality", Organization Studies, 2019
findings.what_they_say: In this account <cite index="52-7">the organization is constituted as a collective actor that is enabled to issue its own acts of speech.</cite> Schoeneborn et al. say <cite index="48-4">some participants, both human and nonhuman, are understood to be the organization's representatives and deemed authoritative.</cite>
findings.note: This is organization-studies work (outside philosophy). It endorses organizations as speakers with hybrid human and nonhuman agency, but is not about LLMs, Kant or Gubelmann's criteria, so it is FRAMEWORK, not ENDORSED.

findings.part: LLM outputs as extensions of collective intentionality rather than an individual's proxy speech
findings.source: "Communicative Action in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Theorizing LLMs as Communicative and Strategic Agents", Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: The paper claims that <cite index="67-10">LLMs are quasi-social agents that perform functional speech acts, which contribute to and extend human collective intentionality.</cite> It also calls LLMs <cite index="67-4">asymmetrical communicative agents satisfying behavioral but not intentional conditions.</cite>
findings.note: PRECEDENT-or-ANTICIPATED is undecided because I saw only abstract and section snippets. It keeps an LLM-level 'behavioral' speaker and does not appear to make the whole the intentional speaker, and I saw no Kantian or organism argument.

findings.part: Layered authorship fixed by a separate attribution rule
findings.source: "Authorship After Generative AI: Distributed Creativity and Relational Responsibility", Philosophy & Technology, 2026 (reporting Floridi 2025 on 'distant writing')
findings.what_they_say: On the Floridi account as reported, <cite index="30-6">authorship does not migrate to the system but is reconfigured at a higher level of abstraction, where it stays normatively attributable to human agents.</cite> The paper also says authorship <cite index="30-3">extends to those who architect, own and profit from the generative infrastructures.</cite>
findings.note: It gives layered attribution but assigns it to humans, not to a whole as speaker. Floridi is seen only secondhand.

findings.part: Authorship and institutional or collective speech acts for artificial agents
findings.source: "Can Artificial Agents be Authors?", Philosophy & Technology, 2025
findings.what_they_say: The paper says <cite index="33-1">the institutional definition of authorship assumes only speech acts with an individual speaker, a consequence of the Searlean account.</cite> Its references include Meijers on collective speech acts.
findings.note: A referee will raise this because it identifies the individual-speaker assumption in authorship accounts. I could not see whether it develops a collective-author view, so the relation is undecided between ADJACENT and PRECEDENT.

findings.part: Most recent syntheses of the proxy, functionalist and relational positions
findings.source: "Who asserts when no one asserts?", Synthese, 2026; "Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models", Philosophy & Technology, 2026; Williams & Bayne, "Chatting with Bots", Inquiry, 2024/2026
findings.what_they_say: The Synthese piece maps functionalist and proxy views. The Philosophy & Technology paper labels <cite index="11-2">dominant approaches properties-based or individualist</cite> and argues <cite index="24-6">assertoric function can persist independently of any bearer of assertoric authority.</cite> Williams & Bayne argue that <cite index="25-3">neither proxy-assertion nor fictionalism is satisfactory</cite>.
findings.note: These are the current reference points a referee will expect the thesis to place itself against. None of the snippets proposes a whole-as-speaker view, but I saw only abstracts and snippets.

findings.part: Proxy accounts may coexist with artificial illocutionary standing
findings.what_they_say: It lists theorists who treat chatbots as instruments, mediators or proxies for human agents, and says <cite index="27-4">proxy status need not exclude artificial illocutionary standing.</cite>
findings.note: It bears on how the thesis distinguishes itself from proxy views, but it is a passing remark, not a developed alternative.

finding.what_is_left: Granting Gubelmann's Kantian criterion and his concession that LLMs have a first step of cognitive autonomy, the criterion does not by itself say whether the relevant individual is the skin-bounded organism or a self-maintaining whole such as a firm. Excluding wholes needs an independent individuation principle, and the autopoietic tradition is the obvious candidate. The thesis owes a defence that maintained human–LLM pipelines in firms meet that principle, or that it is itself biologically parochial. It must also distinguish its view from proxy accounts that already allow organizational or collective principals: the claim is that the LLM is an organ of the speaking whole, not a proxy relaying a principal's intention. On that basis, 'LLMs cannot speak' reduces to 'parts as such do not speak', and the whole's speakerhood plus an attribution rule do the remaining work.
credit: Gubelmann 2024 — gives the organism/mechanism criterion and the material, cognitive and moral autonomy separation, and himself allows that LLMs may be first steps toward non-biological organisms
Green & Michel 2022 and Nickel 2013 — proxy speech, with institutional principals such as a council representative (seen only secondhand)
Arora 2024 — proxy assertion tied to designers or a collective of actors, with the principal's epistemic responsibility
Brummans & Cooren 2014 and Schoeneborn et al. 2019 — organizations as collective actors issuing their own speech acts through human and nonhuman representatives
Weber & Varela 2002 — Kant's natural purposes linked to identity and self-production, which both supplies and constrains the individuation question
The 2026 Habermas-and-speech-act paper — LLM speech acts as extending human collective intentionality (undecided on anticipation)
Floridi 2025 via the 2026 Authorship After Generative AI paper — authorship reconfigured across levels of abstraction
finding.not_found: I found no text that applies Kant's natural-purpose concept to firms or newsrooms as speakers, and none that argues an LLM is an organ of a goal-setting whole. I also found no direct reply to Gubelmann on the skin boundary or biological chauvinism. This is weak evidence given the paywalled literature. Targets and sources I could not check at full text: I saw Green & Michel 2022 only through Gubelmann and other authors, and I saw Gubelmann 2024 only as snippets. I did not check Gubelmann & Toscano 2022 ('Mechanism versus organism') or Kant's own remarks on the state or other wholes as natural purposes. Within philosophy, I did not reach List & Pettit's group-agency work, collective speech-act literature (Meijers appeared only as a reference), or the extended-mind literature. I did leave philosophy: organizational-communication work (CCO, Cooren) and autopoiesis biology and theory. I found no psychology, cognitive science or sociology studies of how people attribute speech acts to firms versus LLMs. A CHI 2025 paper on attribution perceptions in human–AI co-creation (He, Houde, Weisz) appeared only as a reference-list entry and I did not read it.

sep.why: The theses turn on Kant's natural-purpose (organism) criterion, which 'Kant, Immanuel: aesthetics and teleology' covers, on whether a whole such as a firm can hold intentions and act as a collective author, and on what it takes to perform a speech act.

findings.position: Kant's notion of an organism as a 'natural purpose' is the Kantian machinery a criterion like Gubelmann's would draw on. The entry gives the definition and the claim that only organized beings meet it. The text I received breaks off just as it begins to explain what makes an organism a natural purpose, so the part-whole (organ) analysis is not visible to me.
findings.who: Kant (CJ §§64–65), as reported by the entry
findings.quote: organized beings ... instantiate the concept of a natural purpose and also ... they are the only beings in nature that do so (§65, 376)
findings.note: Gives the thesis the Kantian base. The entry also says Kant restricts natural purposes to organisms, which is the 'stopping at the skin' the thesis calls chauvinistic.

findings.position: Kant's distinction between inner and outer/relative objective purposiveness. Organisms have inner purposiveness; one thing standing in a means-end relation to another has only relative purposiveness. This is a resource for treating an LLM as a means or part within a larger goal-directed whole.
findings.who: Kant; treated in detail by Marc-Wogau (1938) and Tonelli (1958), per the entry
findings.quote: this distinguishes the kind of purposiveness possessed by organisms from that in virtue of which one natural thing or process stands in a means-end relation to another
findings.note: The thesis's 'organ of a larger whole' framing can be set against this inner/relative contrast.

findings.position: Purposiveness analysed as conceptually guided design. Artifacts are the paradigm case of purpose, and Teufel reads the ascription of purposiveness as an ontological claim about a rational, conceptually guided origin. This bears on whether a maintained human–LLM pipeline counts as a purposive whole.
findings.who: Kant §10; Teufel (2011); Ginsborg 1997b (normative lawfulness) as a rival reading
findings.quote: an ascription of purposiveness to an object makes an ontological claim to the effect that the object is the outcome of a rational, conceptually guided process
findings.note: A referee would raise the dispute over what Kantian purposiveness requires (design, normativity, or unity of diversity) before accepting the extension to pipelines.

findings.position: Nature as a system of purposes and the human being or culture as ultimate purpose. This is a nearby Kantian whole-and-parts framework, though it concerns nature and morality, not speakers or authors.
findings.quote: the human being, as a free and rational agent, is the "ultimate purpose" [Endzweck] of nature
findings.note: Only the section headings and passing mentions are visible; the body text of 3.5–3.6 is not in what I received.

nearest_positions: Organisms as natural purposes, the only beings that meet the concept (inner objective material purposiveness) — Kant CJ §§64–65, as reported in the entry
Purposiveness as an etiological claim of conceptually guided origin — Teufel (2011), against purposiveness as normative lawfulness (Ginsborg 1997b) or unity of diversity (Zuckert 2007a)
Inner versus relative (means-end) purposiveness — Kant, treated by Marc-Wogau (1938) and Tonelli (1958)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Everything specific to the thesis. The entry never mentions Gubelmann, LLMs, AI, speakerhood or authorship, and nothing on biological chauvinism. It has no discussion of human–AI pipelines as wholes, of layered authorship, of an attribution rule, or of a 'third kind of author'. The visible text does not show Kant's part-whole (organ) analysis of natural purposes, because the entry is cut off at the start of §3.3.

findings.position: Agency is settled by functional conditions, not by biological or individual-organism boundaries. A whole can meet those conditions as a unit, with attitudes that are not those of its parts. This gives the thesis its 'no stopping point at the skin' step and its claim that the whole may be the speaker or author.
findings.who: Pettit (and List & Pettit): groups fulfil conditions of agency 'as collective units of agency whose attitudes may be discontinuous with the attitudes of their members'. Tollefsen and Rovane: rational unity and the intentional stance for groups.
findings.quote: such groups fulfill them as collective units of agency whose attitudes may be discontinuous with the attitudes of their members
findings.note: The entry offers a model of whole-level subjecthood. Its parts are human members, and nothing in it concerns artefacts or LLMs as parts.

findings.position: Subjecthood needs an internal structure that makes the whole a proper target of ascription, such as decision mechanisms and roles. This matches the thesis's 'maintained pipelines' and the 'separate attribution rule' fixing authorship.
findings.who: Pettit (collectivising reason, authoritative majority votes, straw votes); Tuomela (group positions, authority system); Hindriks's status account; French
findings.quote: a group that is to count as a subject of intentional states has to implement an internal structure and in particular a mechanism for decision-making
findings.note: Gives the thesis a vocabulary for a rule that fixes which attitudes count as the whole's. The entry never applies it to non-human components.

findings.position: Intentions at one level derive from intentions at a higher level, so the same act can be attributed at several layers. Roles within a group are functional positions. This is a broader view that the thesis's 'authorship layered across levels' and 'parts as such' would apply.
findings.who: Sellars (we-derivative I-referential intentions); Tuomela (members 'functioning in group positions')
findings.quote: My intention to move a pawn on the chessboard is derivative from our intention to play a game of chess.
findings.note: Layering of attitudes is present, but only among human individuals. Nothing in the entry treats a part as an organ lacking intentionality of its own.

findings.position: The Individual Ownership Claim and the internalist and naturalist versions hold that all intentionality is the individual's own and settled by features inside individual minds. A rule fixing the skin as the boundary is thereby defended. The thesis must answer this rival rather than just accuse it of chauvinism.
findings.who: Searle (intentionality 'inside individuals' heads'); the Individual Ownership Thesis as the entry presents it; Collingwood on society having 'no will but the will of its members'
findings.quote: all the intentionality an individual has is their own (the Individual Ownership Claim)
findings.note: A rival to the 'no principled stopping point' step. It targets the skin boundary only for minds, not for authors.

findings.position: Group agency or authorship is merely metaphorical shorthand for members' attitudes. The thesis's claim that 'the whole may be a speaker' faces this deflationary view.
findings.who: Quinton (1975); Tuomela (groups are agents 'only in a metaphorical sense')
findings.quote: groups can but need not be taken as (singular) entities, and they are agents and persons only in a metaphorical sense
findings.note: Rival to the whole-as-speaker claim. The entry presents it as one view among several, not as closing the matter.

findings.position: The entry notes an alternative to group-as-subject: two or more individuals may jointly form the subject. It also lists Gilbert's neutrality about whether a 'single body' is composed of human beings. These bear on whether the thesis's 'whole' is a distinct kind of subject or a plural arrangement.
findings.quote: the concept of a 'single body' is neutral with respect to the question whether the body in question is in some sense composed of individual human beings
findings.note: A referee would raise this against 'a distinct third kind of author is not established'. It also supports leaving the question open.

nearest_positions: Group agent as a subject in its own right, with attitudes discontinuous with its members — Pettit / List & Pettit (with Tollefsen's interpretationism and Rovane's rational unity)
Individualist and reductionist ontology: groups are agents only metaphorically, and all intentionality is individually owned — Tuomela, Quinton, Searle, Collingwood
Layered, we-derivative intentions and structured group positions — Sellars and Tuomela (we-mode groups as collective artefacts), with Hindriks's status account of corporate agents
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: LLMs, AI systems, or any artefact or tool as part of an agent. Authorship or speaking as opposed to intending. Kant or Gubelmann's criterion. Biological chauvinism. Human–machine pipelines or maintenance. Treating a component as an 'organ' without intentionality of its own. All of the entry's parts are human members.

findings.position: Speech acts depend on the speaker's communicative intentions: the intention must be efficacious and publicly accessible. On Green's view, performing a speech act means overtly committing oneself to a content. This is the sort of requirement a text-generating system would be tested against, and the entry never applies it to machines or to composite agents.
findings.quote: speech acts involve intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment; further, that commitment is not undertaken simply by virtue of my intending to undertake it
findings.note: Gives the criterion for speakerhood that the thesis relocates from the LLM to the whole; the entry does not discuss who or what counts as the agent.

findings.position: The entry's view of speaker meaning is not limited to humans or to a particular biology. Davis's cases (infants, photocopiers, photographs) show speaker meaning does not need ordinary addressee-directed effects. Searle allows a dog to request. Neither case settles whether non-biological or composite systems can speak.
findings.quote: Searle considers the case of a dog requesting to be let outside (1969, p. 39).
findings.note: Mild support for resisting biological chauvinism at the margins; no bearing on LLMs or pipelines.

findings.position: A speech act can be performed by means of other speech acts, and institutional and conventional acts get their force from authority, role and uptake. This gives the thesis materials for a separate attribution rule that is not fixed by the physical performer alone.
findings.who: Searle and Vanderveken 1985 (strong illocutionary commitment); Austin (felicity conditions); Reimer 1995 (illocutionary conventions)
findings.quote: Even in such a case she performs S n only by virtue of intentionally performing some other set of speech acts
findings.note: Layering of acts and role-based attribution exist in the entry, but only for individual speakers, not for wholes composed of parts.

findings.position: Audience-relative manifestness: what a speaker speaker-means can differ across parts of the audience. This shows the entry's willingness to relativise speaker meaning, though not to relativise authorship across levels of a composite agent.
findings.quote: What is manifest to one addressee may not be manifest to another, and a speaker may exploit this fact.
findings.note: A distant analogy for the thesis's 'layered' attribution.

findings.position: Utterance alone, even of a performative sentence, does not make a speech act, as the sleep-talking case shows. This undercuts a purely output-based test of speakerhood and so fits the thesis's turn to a goal-setting whole, but the entry offers no test of its own.
findings.quote: neither a sentence, nor even the utterance of a sentence, is sufficient on its own for the performance of a speech act
findings.note: Supports locating speakerhood in the agent's intentions rather than in the text produced.

nearest_positions: Intentionalism: speech acts require overtly manifested communicative intentions and commitment (Strawson 1964; Green 2013, 2019; Grice 1957)

Force conventionalism: speech acts depend on conventions or constitutive rules, which would let institutional or role-based attribution rules do the work (Austin 1962; Searle 1969; Reimer 1995 on illocutionary conventions)
Davis 1992 and Searle's dog: speaker meaning and requesting without the standard human audience-directed intentions or constitutive rules
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Gubelmann and any Kantian criterion of agency; LLMs or any machine as speaker or author; human–machine pipelines; composite, group or corporate speakers and the 'organ/whole' relation; authorship layered across levels; a 'third kind of author'; and the charge of biological chauvinism. The entry never takes up who the speaker is when parts contribute to an utterance.

theses: Gubelmann's Kantian criterion has no principled stopping point at the skin without biological chauvinism. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines, it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting whole, so 'LLMs cannot speak' reduces to 'parts as such do not speak'. The whole may be a speaker, with authorship layered across levels and fixed by a separate attribution rule. A distinct third kind of author is not established.
